title: Risk Management — Expected Loss, Residual Risk, and Choosing Among the Risk Responses
scenario: Northstar Services is reviewing the ransomware entry on its enterprise risk register. Management estimates an 8% annual probability of a successful attack, with an estimated total loss of $4,500,000 if one occurs. A proposed control package costing $150,000 a year would reduce the annual probability to 2% without changing the loss severity. A cyber insurance policy is also available for a $110,000 annual premium; it reimburses losses above a $500,000 retention up to a $5,000,000 limit. Northstar's total equity is $28,000,000 and its credit agreement contains a fixed-charge coverage covenant. Answer each requirement in complete sentences and show your computations.

exhibits.label: Exhibit A — Ransomware risk register entry

requirements.prompt: Requirement 1 — Compute the inherent expected annual loss, the residual expected annual loss after the control package, and the net annual benefit of implementing the controls. State whether the controls should be implemented and define what residual risk means in this context.

noneOf: no risk remains after the controls

requirements.modelAnswer: Expected loss is probability multiplied by severity. Inherent expected loss is 8% of $4,500,000, or $360,000 a year. After the control package the probability falls to 2%, so residual expected loss is $90,000. The controls therefore cut expected loss by $270,000 while costing $150,000, and the net annual benefit is $120,000, so Northstar should implement the controls. Residual risk is what remains after the response is in place. It matters here because the reduced probability applies to the same $4,500,000 severity: the controls make an attack less likely, but they do not make one survivable, and management is still exposed to a single event that would consume roughly 16% of the $28,000,000 equity base and put the fixed-charge covenant at risk in the year it happened.

requirements.prompt: Requirement 2 — Name the four categories of risk response and identify which response each element of this plan represents. Compute the expected annual cost with controls alone and with controls plus insurance, and explain why buying the policy can be rational even though it raises expected cost.

noneOf: insurance is a risk avoidance response
the policy should never be bought

requirements.modelAnswer: The four responses are avoid, reduce, share or transfer, and accept. Declining to operate the exposed service would be avoidance; the control package is a reduction response; the cyber policy is a risk transfer response that shifts severity to the insurer; and the $500,000 retention plus anything above the limit is acceptance. With controls alone the expected annual cost is $150,000 plus $90,000, or $240,000. Adding insurance costs the $110,000 premium plus 2% of the $500,000 retention, or $10,000, alongside the same $150,000, for $270,000. The policy is therefore $30,000 more expensive in expected value. It is still rational to buy, because expected value ignores the shape of the tail: a single uninsured $4,500,000 event would breach the fixed-charge covenant and consume a sixth of equity, and Northstar cannot absorb that outcome as easily as it can absorb a known premium.
